COMPACT SUBSPACES IN THE SPACE OF SUBGROUPS OF A TOPOLOGICAL GROUP

       I. V. Protasov                                                                 UDC 512.546


      Let G be a topological group, let ~ (G) be the space of its closed subgroups equipped
with the E-topology. The open prebase of this topology is formed by the sets DI(U) = {X C ~ (G
X ~_ U), D2(V) = {X E ~ (O): X N V ~ O } , where U and V run over all open subsets of G. The
structure of topological groups G for which the space ~ (G) or some of its subspaces satisfy
various compactness conditions was studied in [I-7]. At the same time, the topological struc
ture of the space ~(G) itself or its subspaces, in particular, compact ones, has essentially
never been studied. For instance, a characterization of compact spaces homeomorphic to s
for a suitable topological group G is unknown (A. V. Arkhangel'skii's problem).
     The present note the results of which have been announced in [8] obtains a compactness
criterion for subspaces of ~(O) for an arbitrary locally compact group G. The structure of
compact subspaces in the subspaces ~(G) and n~(G) of, respectively, compact and noncompact
subgroups of ~(G) is studied, along with the question when is the topology of the space ~(G)
determined by the family of its compact sets. All studied groups are assumed to be locally
compact, and the word "subgroup" refers only to closed subgroups.
       LEMMA i.    If ~   is a closed countably compact subspace in ~(G), then the subspace K =
U     F is compact in G.


     Proof. We will first show that K is compact. Suppose the contrary. Then there exist a
compact neighborhood U of the identity of the group G and a sequence {Xn} of elements of K
such that xiU n x i U = Z for i = j. For each natural number n we choose a subgroup F n 6 ~ in
such a way that Xn6 Fn. By the countable compactness of ~ , the sequence of subgroups {Fn}
has a limit point P. Since ~ is closed P 6 9 , therefore, P is a compact subgroup. By con-
struction, the subspace X consisting of the elements of the sequence (Xn} is discrete and
closed in G. Thus, X N PU is finite. So there exists a natural number m such that xn ~ P U
for all n > m. But then the neighborhood DI(PU) of the subgroup P does not contain any sub-
groups Fn, n > m. This contradicts the fact that P is a limit point of the sequence {Fn}.
It remains to show that K is closed. Suppose that x 6 K and a directed set {x=), = 6 J , of ele-
ments of K s             to x. For each a 6 J we choose a subgroup F = 6 ~ in such a way that x~ 6
F~. Since K is compact, it follows from Vietoris's theorem (p. 52 in [9]) that one can choos,
in the directed set {Fa}, ~ 6 J , a directed subfamily {F~}, ~6f, converging to some subgroup S.
Since ~ is closed, $ 6 ~       and, therefore, S___K . It follows from the definition of the E-
topology and the construction of the family {F~}, ~61 , that x6 S. Thus, x6 K and the lemma is
proved.

are fulfilled:
     i) ~   is closed;
     2) ~   contains no infinite descending chains of noncompact subgroups;
     3) each closed subspace ~' of ~          contains only finitely many maximal in 9' noncompact
        subgroups;
     4) if a closed subspace ~' of ~ contains no noncompact subgroups, then                      U   F   is compact
         in G.                                                                                  ~'
     Proof. Necessity. Let 9 be a compact subspace in ~(G). Condition i is obvious. Sup-
pose that condition 2 is violated and ~ contains an infinite chain F ~ F2~... of noncompact
subgroups. Since 9 is compact, the sequence {Fn} has a limit point F. It follows from the
definition of the E-topology that F~_Fn for each n, and this contradicts Lemma 2. Suppose
that condition 3 is not fulfilled and the subset 91 of noncompact subgroups maximal in 9' is
infinite. Since ~' is compact, the subset ~i has a limit point H 6 9 ' .     By Lemma 2, there
exists a neighborhood ~ of the subgroup H in ~', consisting of subgroups contained in H.
Choose two distinct subgroups F~ and F 2 in ~.   Then F I ~ H , F 2 ~ H . Since H Eg", the maxi-
mality of the subgroups F~ and F 2 in 9' implies that F~ = F 2. This contradicts the choice
of the subgroups F l and F 2. Finally, condition 4 follows from Lemma I.
       Sufficiency. If 9 ~ ( O ) , then the compactness of 9 follows immediately from condition~
i, 4, and Vietoris' theorem. Suppose that ~ contains noncompact subgorups and put 9 0 = 9 .
Condition i and Lemma 3 in [i] imply that each noncompact subgroup in 90 is contained in a
maximal subgroup in 90. By condition 3, the number of such subgroups is finite. Let F~ .... ,
F n be the noncompact subgroups maximal in 90. Consider an arbitrary covering of 90 with
open sets and choose among them ~i .....~    such that FI~ ~i .....Fn6 ~n. Put ~I = 90~(~i 0 ...~ ~nl
If ~i ~ ~(G), then, by the above, ~i is compact and, thus, ~0 is also compact. Otherwise,
by a similar argument, we construct ~2, etc. We will show that for some natural number m
~m ~ ( G )  and, therefore, ~0 is compact. Suppose the contrary. Then the set ~m of maximal,
in 9m, noncompact subgroups is nonempty and, by condition 3, finite for each natural number
m. Note that for each subgroup K m in ~,~ there exists a chain of subgroups K m ~ K m _ 1 ~ . . . ~ K o ,
where KiC~i, i = 0, I .... ,m. So some subgroup NoE~0 is the end of infinitely many such
chains. Among subgroups of ~, contained in N O there exists a subgroup N l through which in-
finitely many chains pass. Continuing this argument, we construct an infinite descending
chain of subgroups No~NI~... , contrary to condition 2. The theorem is proved.

     A topological space is said to be sparse (in Cantor's sense) if each nonempty subspace
of it contains a point isolated in this subspace.

                                                                                                               513
       COROLLARY 3.     Each compact set ~      in n~(O) is sparse.
     Proof. By Theorem i, ~ contains no infinite descending chains of subgroups. So each
nonempty subspace ~i of ~ contains a subgroup F I minimal in ~i. By Lemma 2, F ! is an iso-
lated point of the subspace ~1-
     Sparse compact spaces possess many remarkable properties although the problem of their
classification has not been solved (cf. [i0]). In connection with Corollary 3, the following
question arises: is it possible to embed each sparse compact space homeomorphically in the
subspac~ n~ (O) for an appropriate group G? Spaces of ordinals admit such a realization.
Moreover, each compact space in the Vietoris exponent expX of a discrete space X can be em-
bedded in n~(O). It is unknown, however, whether each sparse compact space can be realized
in exp X.
      It is worth noting that, for a suitable choice of a group G, each given compact space
can be realized in the space ~(O). This follows from Tikhonov's theorem and the fact that
the space ~(O) of the group O = T • C2 contains a segment (T is the one-dimensional torus,
C 2 is the cyclic group of order 2, x is the symbol of the topological semidirect product).
     The results above demonstrate a substantial difference in topological properties between
the subspaces ~(G) and n~(O). We will give some other examples. ~(O) is locally compact for
each group G (p. 54 in [9]); ~(O) is o-compact if the group G is o-compat [2]; ~(O) satis-
fies the first countability axiom if the group G does. None of these statements is, gener-
ally speaking, true for the subspace n~(G). It follows from Lemma 2 in [2] that n~(G) satis-
fies the first countability axiom if G is a group of countable weight. Thus, for group G of
countable weight both subspaces ~(O) and n~(O) satisfy the first countability axiom. How-
ever, as the following theorem shows, this statement is not, generally, true for the space
~(O). A special case of Theorem 2 is the key Lemma 3 of [6].
     THEOREM 2. If the space ~(G) of a zero-dimensional group G is locally countably com-
pact or satisfies the first countability axiom, then each noncompact inductively compact sub-
group of G is open.
     Proof. Let H be an inductively compact subgroup in n ~(G). By Lemma 2, D!(H) is a neigh
borhood of H in ~(G) . By virtue of its inductive compactness, H belongs to the closure in
the E-topology of the sets of its compact subgroups. Thus, DI(H) is a neighborhood of some
compact subgroup K. By definition of the E-topology, there exist subsets U, V~,...,V n open
in G such that K~_U, KnV1=/=~ .....KnV,=/=~ and the neighborhood ~ =DI(U) ND2(VI)N.-. nD2(Fn)
of the subgroup K is contained in DI(H).
       Suppose that W is an open compact subgroup in G and KW~_U.               We choose a subgroup W l in
such a way that x - I W ~ x ~ W f o r   each x EK.   We denote by W 2 the least subgroup containing U x -~

wlx. Then P = KW 2 is an open subgroup and P C ~          .   Thus, F ~ H   and H is open.   The theorem is
proved.
     A natural class of topological spaces containing locally compact spaces as well as
spaces with the dirst countability axiom is given by the k-spaces, i.e., spaces whose topo-
logy is determined by a family of compact sets (p. 153 in [ii]). It follows from the above
that for a group G of countable weight ~ (G) and n~ (O) are k-spaces. Is ~ (G) a k-space in
this case? For connected solvable Lie groups it is so [7]. An affirmative answer for a
class of groups containing all discrete and inductively pronilpotent groups of countable
weight is given by Theorem 3 whose statement and proof are preceded by two lemmas.
     LEMMA 3. If G is a group of countable weight, then the character of a point H in ~ (G)
in the subspace D~(H) is countable.
       The proof follows from the definition of a base of the E-topology.

     COROLLARY 4. The space s                of   a group G of countable weight is a k-space if one of
these conditions is fulfilled:
        i) G contains an open       compact normal subgroup;
        2) the inductively compact radical of the group G contains all compact elements of G.
     Proof. In the former case the condition that the set of inductively compact subgroups
is closed in s   follows from Lemma 1 in [2], in the latter case it is obvious.
